newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Manuel sees 2.5 pct S.African growth in fiscal '97.
newsitem.headline: Manuel sees 2.5 pct S.African growth in fiscal '97.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said on Tuesday he continued to expect the country to achieve a 2.5 percent growth rate in the 1997/98 fiscal year.
"When we were saying 2.5 percent (in the March budget), there was so much bullishness around that people thought we were being silly," he told a news briefing in Cape Town.
"Many of those people more recently changed their minds and said that the outlook was a lot more morbid. But we think that 2.5 percent for the fiscal year still stands."
Some economists have recently cut their growth forecasts for calendar 1997, primarily citing a slowdown in domestic demand.

Manuel estimated that for the calendar year, inflation would average between 8.9 percent and nine percent. Commenting on prospects for the budget deficit, Manuel said South Africa would be under pressure to meet its target of 4.0 percent of gross domestic product.

"Clearly this was always going to be an exceedingly hard year," he said. "This has to be the year of turnaround (but) there are a number of pressures...It is not going to be easy but we have to ensure that we do in fact hold a pretty tight rein," he said.
Pressures included meeting the wage bill for education departments, which were already heavily overspent in many provinces.
But meetings had been held with the provinces on how to deal with the situation within the framework of the three-year medium term expenditure framework.

"The fact that we are doing it early enough in the fiscal year also assists because we can now understand what the pressures are," he said. "There is no magic about this. There is going to be a lot of interaction to ensure that we do lay a very solid basis."
Undertaking the process this year was also important because this was the first time that the provinces had had greater budgeting powers.
Unions have criticised the government's stringent budget deficit cutting targets. But Manuel said this missed the point that this was a discipline facing all governments in the world.

"There is still going to be a hard slog to ensure that we have policy credibility, but you do that in a way that does not compromise certain fundamentals about transformation and also about living in the world," Manuel said.
"South Africa needs to understand that part of what it needs to do is win market confidence, but that is elusive and we have got to understand the macro-economic constraints."
